frameworks.name: Red-Yellow-Green Delegation Inventory
frameworks.definition: A color-coded categorization system applied to every founder task: green = delegate immediately to existing team; yellow = install a process or one-time project first, then delegate; red = requires a hire or new capability not yet present in the organization.

frameworks.name: Shadow-Supervise-Support Training Sequence
frameworks.definition: A three-stage employee handoff protocol: (1) Shadow — employee watches founder execute; (2) Supervise — founder watches employee execute and provides corrections; (3) Support — founder is available but not involved, and the employee owns the work independently.

frameworks.name: Frustrated Fred vs. Wealthy William Wealth Model
frameworks.definition: A comparative financial model contrasting two $10M-revenue/$2M-profit businesses: one requiring 80 hours/week of founder time (valued at personal income only) versus one fully founder-independent (valued at 6x profit multiple), demonstrating that business independence multiplies net worth non-linearly.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi argues that a business requiring the founder's daily involvement is not a real business in the strategic sense: it creates liabilities, removes optionality, and produces what is effectively a job the founder cannot quit, regardless of revenue or profit.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that a fully founder-independent business generating $2M profit annually is worth approximately $12M (at a 6x profit multiple), while a founder-dependent business generating the same $2M profit accumulates wealth at only ~$500k/year after taxes and living expenses — roughly a 20x net-worth-building speed difference between the two structures.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Both businesses at $10M top line, $2M profit
50% effective tax rate assumed
6x profit multiple for the independent business
claims.mechanism: The independent business is valued on a profit multiple that other investors will pay; income from the dependent business is taxed annually and cannot be monetized via a multiple.

numbers.axis: annual net worth increase per business structure

anchors.value: $12M lump-sum business value at any point of sale

claims.text: Alex Hormozi argues that every incremental $500k of additional annual profit is worth 6x more ($3M added to net worth) in a founder-independent business than in a founder-dependent one ($250k after-tax cash), because the independent business compounds profit through a valuation multiple rather than income.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Fully founder-independent business trading at 6x profit multiple
50% effective tax rate
claims.mechanism: Profit in a sellable business is multiplied by an investor-assigned multiple at the point of sale or valuation, so each incremental dollar of profit generates 6 dollars of net worth rather than 50 cents (after tax).

claims.text: Alex Hormozi contends that the primary way to remove oneself from day-to-day operations is to first conduct a time study — recording every 15-minute block of activity for a full week — to surface an exhaustive list of what the founder actually does, which is then classified as things to delegate, systematize, or hire for.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Applicable to any founder trying to reduce founder-dependency

claims.text: Alex Hormozi argues that decision trees — explicit if-then rules for common recurring scenarios — are the primary mechanism for replacing founder judgment in operational roles, because most recurring questions in a business fall into a finite set of case types that can be documented in advance.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Most applicable to high-volume, repetitive customer-facing or operational functions (e.g., support, billing changes)
claims.mechanism: Recurring decisions decompose into finite case types; documenting each case eliminates the need for founder approval because the answer becomes retrievable rather than judgment-dependent.
bounded_by: More complex or rare one-off scenarios still require human judgment or escalation

claims.text: Alex Hormozi recommends creating financial approval thresholds — a dollar ceiling below which employees can make independent spending or compensation decisions — so that routine service-recovery or operational spending does not route to the founder, while the aggregate pattern remains visible via monthly financials.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Threshold amount scales with company size (example: <$500 for small companies, up to <$100k for larger ones)
bounded_by: Founder still monitors total financial pattern monthly to detect anomalies

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that when employees understand how their specific role contributes to company revenue, it increases their sense of meaning and impact — and that most employees currently cannot articulate this connection.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: Understanding the revenue impact of one's role converts abstract job tasks into quantifiable contributions, giving employees a feedback loop that produces intrinsic motivation and reduces need for founder oversight.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi believes that no single founder can out-work every person in the organization; a founder can out-work any one individual but cannot out-work everyone collectively, making delegation through an organization the only path to Mount-Everest-scale output.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi

claims.text: Alex Hormozi argues that replacing 50 hours/week of doing with 20 hours/week of managing produces a roughly 10x improvement in leverage over one's labor, and that this multiplication compounds with each additional layer of management inserted between the founder and frontline work.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Applies when the founder is the primary doer of the work being delegated
claims.mechanism: Each management layer multiplies the span of productive hours the founder's time controls; one hour of management governs multiple doer-hours rather than the founder performing the work directly.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi measures employee quality by rate of improvement rather than starting skill level, because a lower-starting but faster-improving employee will surpass a higher-starting but slower-improving employee within three to six months and compound that advantage over time.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Applies most clearly in roles where skill can be built through training and repetition, not solely through prior experience
claims.mechanism: A faster learner's improvement trajectory crosses the slower learner's performance line at a predictable point and then diverges further; higher starting performance from experience is a fixed asset while learning rate is a compounding asset.
bounded_by: Role-dependent: some highly technical roles may still require prior experience as a floor

claims.text: Alex Hormozi defines intelligence operationally as the rate at which behavior changes under constant conditions, and uses this definition to prefer faster-learning but less experienced employees over slower-learning but more experienced ones in most roles.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
bounded_by: Role-specific: applies less cleanly to highly technical or credentialed roles

claims.text: Alex Hormozi argues that the quality of a candidate's metrics tracking for their role is the single best proxy for their actual competence in that role: a candidate who can articulate cost-of-hire, time-to-fill, and two-way 90-day fit rates is demonstrably more skilled in talent management than one who cannot.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Most directly applicable to leadership, director-level, and functional expert roles
claims.mechanism: Practitioners who achieve excellent results in a domain are forced by feedback to track the inputs and outputs that drive those results; inability to name those metrics indicates they have not operated at high performance in that domain.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi contends that interviewing a very large number of candidates for a role (e.g., 600 developers interviewed to find one CTO co-founder) is the practical mechanism for calibrating judgment about who is good in that role, because pattern recognition only develops after exposure to enough contrasting examples.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Particularly relevant for senior or specialized roles where the founder has not previously hired
Volume approach scales down for junior roles via group interviews
claims.mechanism: Interviewing many candidates in the same role builds a comparative mental model; the tenth interview begins to distinguish genuine skill from performance, and by the fiftieth a reliable internal benchmark exists.

anchors.value: meaningful comparative signal begins to emerge
reliable picker calibrated for the role

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that for leadership-level roles and above, the interview should be a learning experience for the founder — if the founder is not learning from the candidate, the candidate is not senior enough to fill that leadership role and will require net training investment rather than providing net expertise.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Applies to director-level and above
Does not apply to frontline or mid-level roles where training by the founder is expected
claims.mechanism: A senior hire's value is the knowledge and systems they bring that the founder lacks; if the founder is more knowledgeable than the candidate, hiring creates a net training burden and delays capability development.
bounded_by: Frontline to manager-level: founder-led training is expected and acceptable

claims.text: Alex Hormozi argues that founder-driven marketing and customer acquisition is the biggest single risk factor for a founder's ability to exit day-to-day operations, because when the founder is the promoter, revenue declines directly and visibly upon founder absence.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Particularly acute in face-driven or personality-driven brands
claims.mechanism: Brand attention, trust, and acquisition are tied to the founder's personal credibility and presence; removing the founder severs the primary trust signal that converted customers.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi identifies seven categories of founder-independent marketing systems that generate ads and social proof without direct-to-camera founder involvement: community screenshots, testimonial incentive programs, lifecycle ads from CRM recordings, client milestone documentation, customer support testimonial collection, platform review repurposing (Google/Yelp/Amazon), and affiliate or TikTok Shop programs.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Assumes the business already has customers with documented journeys in a CRM
Most applicable to service and product businesses with existing customer touchpoints

numbers.axis: number of founder-independent marketing system categories

claims.text: Alex Hormozi argues that a business has achieved genuine founder-independence only when it can grow — not just maintain — for three months with the founder entirely absent and the founder's phone silent, and uses this as the litmus test before opening a second location.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Particularly applicable to brick-and-mortar businesses considering a second location
Three-month period is the minimum test duration
claims.mechanism: Flat performance during founder absence typically indicates residual founder dependency ('eye of Sauron' effect); the business may decline without the founder's presence redirecting attention and energy.
bounded_by: Businesses in supply-constrained markets where growth is structurally capped by factors other than the founder may stay flat without it indicating dependency

claims.text: Alex Hormozi contends that over-expansion — adding a second location or division before the first unit can grow independently — is one of the primary reasons businesses fail, because it doubles overhead and debt while halving talent concentration, producing more risk and less profit simultaneously.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Applies when the original unit is still founder-dependent or flat during founder absence
claims.mechanism: Expansion before independence spreads management attention across two units, neither of which has autonomous leadership, causing both units to underperform while fixed costs double.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi uses an 80% performance standard as the acceptable initial threshold for a delegated employee: a delegated employee who performs at 80% of the founder's level on a task while the founder is fully absent generates net value, as long as there is a clear improvement path toward higher performance over time.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Initial handoff phase only
Founder must have a documented improvement path for the employee, not just accept 80% as the terminal state

numbers.axis: acceptable employee performance vs. founder baseline at handoff

anchors.value: approaching or exceeding founder level over time

claims.text: Alex Hormozi argues that a belief that no one can do a task as well as the founder is only true on a short time horizon with equal training investment; given full-time dedication, a skilled employee who learns only the correct approaches (without the founder's trial-and-error mistakes) may reach 50% competency immediately and exceed the founder over a longer period.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: A full-time employee who learns the role with structured guidance avoids the years of error-based learning the founder spent; their dedicated focus accelerates their trajectory past the founder's part-time involvement in that task.

numbers.axis: employee starting competency relative to founder

anchors.region: with full-time dedicated focus over time
anchors.value: can exceed founder who now applies partial attention

examples.text: Alex Hormozi described building Prestige Labs, his supplement company, where the customer support manager said it was hard to onboard new support reps. Hormozi challenged this by enumerating what support reps actually handle: change address, change card, change flavor, change billing cadence, cancel, refund. By naming each scenario as a simple if-then case, the supposedly complex onboarding reduced to a decision tree. The example illustrates that even roles that feel complex to document often decompose into a finite set of case types once enumerated.

For School, the education platform, Sam Parr interviewed 600 developers over approximately one year — each a 30-to-60 minute conversation — before finding Daniel, the CTO co-founder. Hormozi uses this example to illustrate that calibrating judgment on senior technical hires requires exposure to a very large comparison set; only after dozens of interviews does the pattern of who is genuinely skilled versus who performs well in interviews become reliably distinguishable.

When Alex Hormozi hired his first strong HR professional, she arrived at the interview and immediately asked him questions he could not answer: What is your cost of acquiring talent? What is your time to fill? What percentage of 90-day placements are rated 10/10 by both the employee and manager? Hormozi realized he had been operating on a talent-equivalent of vanity metrics (no lawsuits lately = good culture) rather than real performance indicators. This example illustrates his claim that a senior hire's quality is revealed by the sophistication of the metrics they track for their own function.

Hormozi described a hotel scenario to illustrate financial approval thresholds: a guest has a bad stay. Under what conditions can the front-desk employee issue a gift card or credit without routing to the founder? The answer depends on company size — the threshold might be $500 for a small company, $10k or even $100k for a larger one. Once set, the employee resolves the issue independently and the founder reviews aggregate financials monthly rather than approving each instance.

Hormozi gave the example of a camera operator to demonstrate how to make any role's revenue contribution legible: bad camera work wastes the whole team's time, causes media underperformance (off-center shots, bad lighting), destroys footage, and creates ill-fitted equipment usage. Reversing these mistakes into positive metrics — percentage of files saved correctly, named correctly, timestamped accurately, lighting set up, start-on-time rate — converts an abstract support role into a trackable revenue-contributor. When all metrics are 100%, the employee is making the company money and understands how.

practices.text: Run a time study for one full week before attempting to delegate: set a 15-minute timer, record one or two words describing what you did each interval in an Excel sheet, and use the resulting list as the inventory of everything you currently do.

Apply the Red-Yellow-Green framework to your complete task inventory: assign green (delegate now to existing team), yellow (install a process or project first, then delegate), and red (need a hire you don't yet have). Resolve greens first, then yellows, then reds.

Ask every team member: 'How does your role make the company money?' Use the answer (or inability to answer) as a diagnostic for whether employees understand their role's value contribution and as a trigger to explain and document that linkage.
Use the Shadow-Supervise-Support handoff sequence for every delegated role: you do it in front of them, they do it in front of you, then they do it independently with you available but not involved.

Set up community screenshot processes, testimonial unlock incentives (trial tier access), lifecycle CRM ad compilation, client milestone documentation, customer support testimonial bounties ($5 per chat testimonial collected), platform review repurposing, and affiliate or TikTok Shop programs as founder-independent marketing systems.
Use group interviews for frontline to manager-level roles to save time and quickly read candidate energy and relative quality in a single session.

Measure employees on rate of improvement, not starting performance level; track whether a newer lower-starting employee is on a trajectory to surpass a more experienced slower-improving one within three to six months.
Take a genuine 90-day absence from the business after you believe you have delegated sufficiently; something will break, and the breaks reveal the remaining founder dependencies to fix.
